prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Bless Tuesday, blessed Monday. Bless the word week, its seven small days trail with y. Bless the men whose words I was too young to hear. A whisper loves a canal. Bless my laugh, lent by grief, I have so little left to borrow. But my hair, it grows— if hair be gold, cut mine so I might rid my beloved of his student loans. Bless thieves, universities, those hands caress what’s not theirs. Bless thinking it was yours. Here are hands, blessed one. Bless them holding the door. Bless each crier on the F train before and after me as they blush, as they transfer into tunnels for the red line. Oh bless, bless wildly, what remains to be done. Bless the one who told me so, the ones who didn’t. Even weak breaths bless. Bless weakness, fragile fortress, my friend’s body absent of soundness. Bless the sound of someone reliable answering your call, saying If you’re going through hell, Hello.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Bless, Tuesday, Monday

outputs.L1:
Because this is a deeply lyrical and poetic text, turning it into standard corporate prose would strip away its beauty. Instead, "professional and eloquent" in this context means **elevating the literary cadence, refining the vocabulary, and smoothing the transitions** while keeping every theme, detail, and emotion intact.

Here are three polished options depending on the exact tone you prefer:

### Option 1: Refined Literary Prose (Recommended)
*Elevates the language and flow while maintaining the original poetic intimacy.*

> "Bless Tuesday; bless Monday. Bless the word *week*, whose seven modest days all trail off in a *y*. Bless the men whose wisdom I was too young to absorb—a whisper loves a canal. Bless my laughter, lent to me by grief, for I have so little left to borrow. Yet my hair continues to grow; if hair were gold, I would shear mine to free my beloved from his student loans. Bless thieves and universities—hands that caress what is not theirs. Bless the sweet illusion of believing it was yours. 
> 
> Here are hands, my blessed one. Bless them as they hold the door. Bless each soul who weeps on the F train, before and after me, blushing as they transfer through dark tunnels toward the Red Line. Oh, bless—bless wildly—all that remains to be done. Bless the one who warned me, and those who stayed silent. Even a frail breath bestows a blessing. Bless weakness, that fragile fortress; bless my friend’s body, now bereft of health. And bless the sound of a steadfast voice answering your call, saying: *‘If you’re going through hell—hello.’*”

---

### Option 2: Elegant & Rhythmic (Poetic Focus)
*Enhances the natural musicality and phrasing of the original text.*

> "Bless Tuesday, and blessed Monday. Bless the word *week*, its seven short days trailing in *y*. Bless the men whose words I was too young to comprehend; a whisper longs for its canal. Bless my laughter, borrowed from grief, when I have so little left to pledge. But my hair still grows—and if hair were gold, I would cut mine to rid my beloved of his debts. Bless thieves, bless universities, bless the hands that hold what isn't theirs. Bless the grace of thinking it was yours. 
> 
> Here are hands, blessed one. Bless them holding open the door. Bless every crier on the F train, before and after my turn, as they blush and transfer through the tunnels for the Red Line. Oh, bless—bless wildly—whatever remains to be done. Bless the one who told me so, and the ones who kept quiet. Even weak breaths carry a blessing. Bless weakness, a fragile fortress, and my friend’s body absent of soundness. Bless the sound of someone reliable answering your call, saying: *‘If you’re going through hell, hello.’*”

---

### Option 3: Modern & Polished (Clean & Direct)
*A subtly smoothed version that fixes minor grammatical rough edges while staying very close to the original text.*

> "Bless Tuesday, blessed Monday. Bless the word *week*, its seven small days trailing off in 'y'. Bless the men whose words I was too young to hear; a whisper loves a canal. Bless my laugh, lent by grief, though I have so little left to borrow. But my hair grows—and if hair were gold, I would cut mine to relieve my beloved of his student loans. Bless thieves and universities, those hands that caress what isn't theirs. Bless thinking it was yours. 
> 
> Here are hands, blessed one. Bless them holding the door. Bless each crier on the F train, before and after me, as they blush and transfer into tunnels for the Red Line. Oh bless, bless wildly, all that remains to be done. Bless the one who told me, and the ones who didn’t. Even weak breaths bless. Bless weakness, that fragile fortress, and my friend’s body, absent of soundness. Bless the sound of someone reliable answering your call, saying, *‘If you’re going through hell, hello.’*”

---

### Key Adjustments Made:
* **Punctuation & Flow:** Corrected comma splices and adjusted sentence structures so the text reads smoothly aloud.
* **Elevated Diction:** Subtle shifts (e.g., *absent of soundness* to *bereft of health*, *rid my beloved of his student loans* to *free my beloved from his student debts*) enhance the elegance without changing the meaning.
* **Formatting the Ending:** Formatted the final punchline (*"If you're going through hell, Hello"*) to emphasize its tragicomic warmth.
outputs.L2:
May grace fall upon Monday and Tuesday, as well as the concept of the seven-day cycle itself, whose brief daily names all terminate with the letter 'y.' Send favor to the older men whose advice was spoken when I was too youthful to comprehend it. A soft voice travels naturally through a narrow passage. Consecrate my laughter, which has merely been loaned to me by sorrow, leaving me with virtually no emotional reserves left to draw upon. 

Yet my tresses continue to lengthen; if these locks held the value of gold, I would shear them completely to erase the debt my partner owes for higher education. Praise be to robbers and academic institutions alike, whose fingers handle property that is not theirs, and praise the mistaken belief that any of it was ever truly yours. 

Look upon these hands, sacred entity; consecrate them as they prop open entryways for others. Offer grace to every passenger weeping on the F train who came before or will follow me, acknowledging their embarrassed, flushed faces as they move through subterranean passageways to switch to the red line. Unreservedly bestow favor on every single unfinished task that remains to be completed. 

Bless the individual who shared the truth with me, along with those who kept quiet. Even the faintest exhalations carry holy weight. Honor frailty—that delicate shield—and the ailing, unsound frame of my companion. Lastly, praise the comforting noise of a dependable person picking up your phone call to offer a warm greeting, even while you navigate through torment.
outputs.L3:
There is a quiet, radical grace to be found in the simple, unrelenting passage of time and the familiar rhythms of daily routine. To offer a blessing to these ordinary moments—and even to the forgotten words left behind in the archives of our past—is to make peace with the impermanence of existence, finding sacredness in the very machinery of living.

Yet, this gentle acceptance is often tested by the heavy reality of personal grief. In the shadows of shared suffering, true devotion reveals itself not in grand, abstract gestures, but in a selfless longing to relieve practical burdens. Amidst the weight of loss, there arises a fierce desire to sacrifice anything of personal value—to surrender every comfort, treasure, or piece of pride—if only it could lift the crushing financial anxieties pressing down upon a beloved, granting them room to breathe and heal.

This capacity for empathy naturally extends outward, bestowing grace upon the raw breadth of human vulnerability. It honors the stranger who displays public sorrow on a crowded commuter train, acknowledging that weeping in the open is not a weakness, but a profound testament to our shared capacity for pain. In the same spirit, physical weakness, illness, and the increasingly fragile bodies of those we love are embraced with tenderness. These states of decay and ailment are not viewed as failures, but as delicate, sacred conditions that demand our deepest compassion and care.

Ultimately, in a world marked by bodily frailty and inevitable loss, true solace is not found in the total absence of pain. Instead, it is discovered in the presence of steady, reliable human connections. When everything else feels uncertain, it is the quiet, unyielding support of one another that anchors us, transforming shared suffering into a landscape of profound tenderness and quiet hope.
outputs.L4:
**The Sanctuary of Small Grace**

There are seasons in human life when trouble does not arrive in single, manageable waves, but as a dense and suffocating tide. In these shadows, one finds oneself weighed down by a triad of exhaustion: the aching, quiet void of grief; the cold, sharp panic of financial scarcity; and the sudden, humbling fragility of a body that no longer yields to the will. To carry all three at once is to feel utterly undone, stripped of the illusion that we are the master architects of our own fates.

When the world collapses to this degree, standard platitudes fail. Advice to "stay positive" feels like a cruel dismissal of real pain. In the depths of such a season, I found that the only way forward was not to fight the weight, but to alter my relationship with it entirely. I began to practice what can only be described as radical affirmation—the deliberate act of bestowing sacred blessings upon the ordinary, the broken, and the mundane.

It started with the smallest routines. In the morning, trembling from physical exhaustion and anxious about the stack of overdue bills waiting on the counter, I would hold a warm cup of water and silently whisper, *Blessed is this heat. Blessed is this breath.* I began to treat the basic mechanics of survival—making a bed, washing a cracked plate, walking slowly down the hallway—not as chores to be endured, but as holy rituals. By sanctifying these small moments, I built tiny islands of peace in a sea of overwhelming uncertainty.

Gradually, this practice expanded from the mundane to the acute. I forced myself to bless the very things I feared and resented. *Blessed be this grief, for it measures the depth of my love. Blessed be this thin wallet, for it strips away my hubris. Blessed be this fragile, aching body, for it forces me to slow down and listen.* This was not a denial of suffering, nor was it toxic optimism. It was an act of radical acceptance. To bless something is to honor its existence without demanding that it immediately change. 

In doing so, a profound paradox began to unfold: embracing my utter weakness did not destroy me; instead, it forged an unexpected fortress of resilience. For years, I had believed that strength meant armor, rigidity, and the unyielding ability to endure pain without flinching. But iron breaks under enough pressure. True resilience, I discovered, is much softer. It is built when we drop our defenses, admit our utter helplessness, and allow ourselves to feel the full weight of our reality. By stopping the energy-draining battle against my own circumstances, I found a quiet, immovable strength hidden at the very center of my vulnerability.

Yet, even the deepest internal practice of self-affirmation has its limits. A fortress, no matter how resilient, cannot be inhabited in total isolation. Perhaps the most vital revelation born of this dark season was the undeniable reality that we are not meant to survive life’s crucible alone. 

Embracing weakness required me to unlearn the pride of self-reliance. It meant opening the door to others—allowing friends to bring a hot meal, accepting a helping hand up the stairs, and being honest about my terror and financial distress. Human connection, reliable support, and the willingness to let ourselves be held by others are not mere luxuries; they are the bedrock of human endurance. The blessings I spoke in solitude were amplified tenfold when echoed by the voices of those who showed up to hold my hand in the dark.

Life does not become easy simply because we change our posture toward it. The grief still visits, the bills must still be paid, and the body remains a temporary, delicate vessel. But by bestowing grace upon the mundane, affirming our deepest struggles, and reaching out to the community around us, we find that suffering loses its power to destroy. In the end, we do not survive life by becoming unbreakable, but by allowing our breaks to become the very places where grace and connection enter in.
outputs.L5:
There is a quiet magic in the way a week begins to unfold. For many, **Monday** arrives like a sudden wave—demanding our attention, resetting our routines, and pulling us away from the slow, restful rhythm of the weekend. It is often a day of heavy lifting, quick adjustments, and running to catch up with the pace of the world. 

But then comes **Tuesday**. 

If Monday is the sudden start, Tuesday is the moment we finally catch our balance. The initial frenzy fades, leaving behind a clear path forward. It is on Tuesday that true focus takes hold. We are no longer reacting to the shock of a new week; we are actively engaging with it, finding our rhythm, and turning our plans into progress. 

It is a wonderful thing to pause and **bless** this middle ground. To bless a day is to wrap it in intention, gratitude, and hope. When we ask for peace to bless our Tuesday, we transform a mundane weekday into a meaningful journey. We honor the resilience it took to cross the bridge of Monday, and we give ourselves permission to move through today with steady confidence and light hearts.

May this day **bless** you with clarity for your tasks, kindness in your interactions, and a deep sense of purpose. As the week builds its momentum, remember that every small effort counts. Let go of yesterday's stress, embrace the possibilities of today, and let a spirit of gratitude guide your steps all through this Tuesday.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem framed as a litany of blessings ("Bless the..."). Focus on the juxtaposition of mundane urban life (like commuting on the F train), modern financial stress (student loans), and deep personal grief or friendship.
counterfactuals.output:
Bless the turnstile that catches on my hip and bless the screech of the F train grinding its iron teeth into the dark curve beneath the East River. Bless the sixty damp strangers pressed shoulder-to-shoulder in the fluorescent glare, the wet wool and ozone, the woman asleep against the scratched plexiglass with her thumb hooked in a canvas tote. Bless the orange plastic seats worn smooth by a million tired spines, and bless the cold drip from the tunnel ceiling that lands precisely on my collar as we idle between stations, waiting for a signal that never comes.

Bless the monthly auto-pay notification arriving at 3:00 AM like a polite mugging in my inbox. Bless Nelnet and Great Lakes, the compound interest bloom like black mold in the corners of my youth, and the thirty-year mortgage I hold on a degree that taught me the word *elegy* but not how to pay for a root canal. Bless the forty-three dollars left in my checking account, the half-eaten block of bodega cheese, and the quiet, absurd arithmetic we do while standing in line at the register—subtracting tax, subtracting dignity, counting the copper in our pockets to see if we can afford to stay alive in a city that charges for the air.

And bless you, my dear friend, who used to split a two-dollar slice with me on the platform when we were both too poor to ride the fast train home. Bless the voice memo from 2019 still saved on my phone, your laughter tinny and bright over the roar of the exhaust fans, before the diagnosis, before the hospital bed, before the swift and terrible silence that took you out of the world. Bless the empty space beside me on this pole where your hand should be, and bless the grief that sits in my lap like an overpacked suitcase, heavy and unshiftable, taking up a seat no one else dares to claim.

Bless the living who keep tapping their MetroCards, stepping over the gap, carrying their secret, unbearable losses through the subterranean gloom. Bless the petty debts we owe to the banks, which are small and stupid, and bless the grand, unpayable debt we owe to those we loved and lost—a debt that compounds in tears, paid out in breath, the only thing that keeps us soft inside this iron cage as the doors open and we step out into the rain.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary poem repeating the word "Bless" that turns sorrow and everyday struggles into a form of gratitude.
counterfactuals.output:
Bless the 6:00 AM alarm, sharp as broken glass.  
Bless the burnt toast, the bitter sludge at the bottom of the mug.  
Bless the cold rain slanting hard against the windshield,  
and bless the red lights that hold me hostage in the turn lane,  
forcing my frantic hands to finally let go of the wheel.  

Bless the bad knee that knows when the season is changing.  
Bless the mail sitting unopened on the counter—  
the bill with the glass window, the numbers that do not balance.  
Bless the fact that there is a roof above the paper.  
Bless the silence in the apartment after the door slams,  
and bless the door for keeping the storm outside.  

Bless the sharp edge of a memory that arrives uninvited.  
Bless the weeping in the parked car, engine idling,  
head pressed against the steering wheel until the horn hums.  
Bless those tears—salt of the earth, salt of my own making—  
washing the dust from eyes that have looked too long at sorrow.  

Bless the heartbreak that left a jagged hole in my chest,  
for bless the empty space that now lets the air back in.  
Bless the scars, those silver threads binding my skin,  
proof that I was cut, proof that I was sewn,  
proof that the body remembers how to heal itself in the dark.  

Bless the ache in my lower back from carrying what wasn't mine.  
Bless the text message that never got a reply.  
Bless the cold floorboards under my bare feet at midnight,  
and bless the water I drink straight from the tap,  
cool and sudden and plain.  

Bless the ruin. Bless the rebuilding.  
Bless the heavy coat I wear against the wind,  
and bless the wind for trying to strip it away—  
reminding me I am still underneath it,  
stubborn, warm, and alive.  

Bless the end of this hard, ordinary day.  
Bless the hands that hold it, empty and full at once.  
Bless the breathing in. Bless the breathing out.  
Bless the staying. Bless the beginning again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem in the lyrical style of poets like Ross Gay or Ocean Vuong, blending themes of grief, NYC transit, student loan debt, fragile bodies, and human connection.
counterfactuals.output: Underground, the interest compounds in the quiet arithmetic of small things, six cents added to my name while the uptown 2 train screams around the curve at 14th Street. I have pledged thirty years of my knuckles to a company whose name sounds like a soft, midwestern river, though it holds my future in an invisible, silver vise—$78,000 for the vocabulary to name my own aching, while my mother, who never learned the word *amortization*, lies beneath six feet of Queens topsoil, entirely debt-free at last. Look at us, gathered in the dim, rattling belly of this iron beast: a gallery of subterranean grace. Here is the nurse with salt-stained boots asleep against the acrylic glass; here is the boy in the damp parka whose headphones leak a synth beat so loud his pulse seems to vibrate outside his skin; here is the old man cradling a bunch of bodega tulips wrapped in wet paper. My hip presses into a stranger’s hip as the car lurches, and neither of us moves away. We are too soft for pride, our bodies merely sackcloth and salt, bruised by turnstiles and the long haul of staying upright. When I pull out my phone to check the account balance that keeps me awake until three in the morning, the blue light catches the reflection of the woman standing over me, her pale wrist hanging from the overhead strap like a loose ribbon, fragile enough to snap under the weight of a single bad winter. In the dark window, her shadow merges with mine, and for a second, I cannot tell whose breath is fogging the glass. I want to tell her that I still buy two coffees every morning out of habit, that grief is just an interest rate that never stops accruing, that my knees already hurt when the rain comes in off the Hudson. But the brakes squeal, the train lurches into the dark between stations, and when she loses her balance, I reach out—my hand just a small, imperfect machine of skin and bone—and catch her by the elbow. We sway together in the damp, crowded heat, two bankrupt ghosts holding each other steady beneath the city, where none of us are solvent, but for a moment, none of us are lost.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a bittersweet benediction for modern life that touches on aging, subway rides, a friend's illness, and a phone call that subverts the phrase "If you're going through hell."
counterfactuals.output:
Blessed be the gentle erosion of time:
the silver stray hairs left in the porcelain sink, 
the dull ache in the knees when taking the stairs, 
and the quiet, startling realization that you are no longer the youngest person in the room, 
nor the most invincible. 

Blessed be the subterranean daily commute—
the swaying, packed subway car at six o’clock, 
where a hundred exhausted strangers grip the same cold pole,
breathing in the heat of each other's tired lives,
watching our own reflections in the dark glass of the tunnel
until the suddenly blinding, glorious burst of street-level light.

Blessed be the fragile bonds that pull us through the grid. 
Blessed be the sterile quiet of waiting rooms, the smell of antiseptic, 
and the sudden, terrifying magnitude of a friend’s diagnosis—
a love that grows impossibly larger even as her body grows small.

And blessed be the vibration of the phone in your palm on a rainy afternoon, 
the crackle of the speaker, and the weak, familiar voice on the line—
the one who rewrites the old, stubborn wisdom. 

When she says: 
*“You know what they say—‘If you’re going through hell, keep going.’*
*But I’m so tired of marching.*
*If you’re going through hell, darling, don’t keep going.*
*Pull over to the shoulder. Turn off the engine.*
*Sit on the hot ground and rest.*
*Call me, and I’ll come bring you a glass of water.”*

So may you forgive your body for modernizing, for weakening, for wearing out. 
May you offer your seat on the train, and may someone offer theirs to you. 
And when the flames rise, may you have the courage to stop walking, 
to sit down in the middle of the dark, 
and discover that you were never meant to cross it alone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a modern, emotional poem about navigating grief, debt, and public transportation using repetitive phrases starting with "Bless"?
counterfactuals.output:
Bless the turnstile that takes my last three dollars.
Bless the red notification on my banking app, a tiny, bleeding eye.
Bless the 7:15 bus, screeching its wet brakes against the curb,
and bless the doors that slide open like a confession.

Bless the plastic seat, still warm from a stranger.
Bless the ghost of you that sits beside me anyway,
wearing the coat I haven't had the heart to wash,
whispering thoughts I can no longer afford to hold.

Bless the tap-to-pay reader that pauses before it accepts my card.
Bless the interest rates, compounding like the silence in your empty room.
Bless the final notices stacked on my kitchen table,
bless the medical bills for a life they couldn't save,
and bless the irony of owing so much for a body that is no longer here.

Bless the flickering fluorescent light overhead.
Bless the commuter to my left, sleeping against the smudged window.
Bless the commuter to my right, staring at a phone she cannot pay either.
Bless the shared, quiet terror of surviving in a city that charges for breathing.

Bless the fog on the window where I trace your initials, then erase them.
Bless the driver’s voice over the crackling speaker, announcing stops I don't want to make.
Bless the dark sunglasses hiding my swollen eyes at eight in the morning.
Bless the woman across the aisle who sees my shaking hands and quietly offers a tissue,
and bless her, especially, for looking away right after.

Bless the overdraft fee—a penalty for being too poor to grieve in peace.
Bless the heavy backpack, filled with thrifted clothes and unpaid promises.
Bless the track steel humming beneath my boots,
a steady, metallic heartbeat for those of us whose hearts have stopped.

Bless the missed stop because I was staring into the void.
Bless the extra blocks I have to walk in the rain.
Bless this exhaustion, heavy as wet wool.
Bless the broke, broken, aching work of carrying on,
and bless my feet, still moving, as I step off into the day.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
